doc.title: Orrin Evans interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

chapter: The barber shop and Uncle's saxophone
title: Uncle the saxophonist hands him the saxophone
summary: On the day they moved in, his uncle gave him the saxophone to carry; the uncle then fell ill and never played again, and Evans fell in love with music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Did you see your uncle operating on gigs?

Um hum. Yeah. But an ironic interesting story. The day we moved to Philadelphia, it was a quick move. So we got to my uncle’s house and we were going to move in with my uncle. He was on the road. And so we were there for two days with him not being there, which was a little weird for me because you didn’t want to touch anything, you’re just sitting around. When he came home I was sitting there in the middle of the floor watching TV. So he came in with his saxophone. And I hadn’t really discovered — I played the piano but I hadn’t fallen in love with music yet. And he came in with his piano player and he looked at me and I looked back at him. He was like, “Here, put this in my room.” And it was his saxophone. So I took the saxophone and I just walked it back to his room. My uncle never played the saxophone again. He ended up getting diagnosed with cancer and never played again. And from that he lost his teeth so he never played — I never heard my uncle play the saxophone again from that moment. But I fell in love with music that next month when I started at the new school. So I always look at it like he was

handing that over to me. And I mean that was — he didn’t even pass until ’95 and that was maybe ’86, so ten years he struggled with it, but he wouldn’t play, which was so weird to me because I was falling in love with music at the time and you know, I’m like how could you not play? But then I also under — he would sit down and play the piano and it was so great when he did, I would turn off everything. But you couldn’t act like you were listening you know what I mean? You just walked and go somewhere else and you’d check him out. So that whole process was really special to me, and I’ll always remember that it was like, “Here, take this to the room.” And whatever was on — mojo was on that saxophone, you know, jumped on me, and I really got into music from that point.
